lessonTitle: Autosomal and X-linked Inheritance: Pedigrees and Recurrence Risk

blocks.text: A mother brings her 5-year-old son to clinic: he has difficulty climbing stairs and has calf muscles that look unusually large. She mentions that her brother died in his teens of 'the same muscle disease', although her parents, her sister and her husband are all well. Within one drawing of the family tree, the pattern of who is affected can point to the gene's location and the risk for the next baby.

blocks.markdown: **Mendelian inheritance** describes the transmission of traits determined by a single gene. A gene on one of the 22 pairs of **autosomes** has two copies in every person; a gene on the **X chromosome** has two copies in females and one in males (males are **hemizygous**). A condition is **dominant** if one mutant allele is enough to produce it in a heterozygote, and **recessive** if two mutant alleles (a homozygote, or in males an X-linked mutant) are needed. Clinicians record the family history as a **pedigree**, a standardised family tree, and read the pattern of affected individuals to infer the mode of inheritance.

rows: Dot in the centre of a symbol (or half-shaded)

blocks.title: Turning a family history into a pedigree
blocks.prompt: The boy in the hook (age 5) has an X-linked muscle disorder. His mother is unaffected; her brother died aged 19 of the same disorder; his maternal grandparents, his sister and his father are unaffected. Describe how each person would be drawn.

steps.text: Generation I: the maternal grandfather (square) and grandmother (circle), joined by a horizontal mating line. Neither is affected, but the grandmother must be a carrier because she passed the allele to both her son and, probably, her daughter.

Generation II: the mother (circle, with a central dot as she is a probable carrier), her deceased brother (filled square with diagonal line) and her husband (open square). Her brother and she are drawn as children of generation I.

Generation III: the proband, the 5-year-old boy (filled square with an arrow) and his unaffected sister (open circle, potential carrier). Siblings are drawn in birth order from left to right under the parents' line.
Because the disease passed from the maternal grandmother (carrier) to her son and then via his sister (mother) to her son, with no male-to-male transmission, an X-linked recessive pattern is likely.

blocks.answer: Three generations with a filled arrow-marked square for the proband, a dotted circle for the carrier mother, and a filled deceased square for the uncle; the pattern suggests X-linked recessive inheritance.

blocks.markdown: **Autosomal dominant (AD).** Affected people appear in every generation (*vertical transmission*). Males and females are equally affected and can both transmit the condition, including **male-to-male transmission**. An affected heterozygote has a 50% chance of transmitting the mutant allele to each child. Unaffected people do not pass the condition on (apart from non-penetrance or new mutations). Examples: Marfan syndrome, familial hypercholesterolaemia, Huntington disease. **Autosomal recessive (AR).** Affected people are usually in a single generation (*horizontal pattern*, siblings affected), with unaffected parents who are carriers. Males and females are equally affected. Consanguinity (parents related) increases the likelihood. Examples: phenylketonuria, Wilson disease, sickle cell disease. The risk for each child of two carriers is **1 in 4** affected, **1 in 2** carrier and **1 in 4** unaffected non-carrier.

**X-linked recessive (XLR).** Males are affected far more often than females; the trait is passed from carrier females (who are usually unaffected or mildly affected) to **half of their sons**, and half of their daughters are carriers. An affected father has no affected sons because he passes his Y to them (**no male-to-male transmission**), but all his daughters are obligate carriers. Examples: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, haemophilia A, red-green colour blindness. **X-linked dominant (XLD).** Affected fathers pass the trait to **all daughters and no sons**; affected mothers transmit to half of children of either sex. Affected females are more common than males, and hemizygous males are often more severely affected. An example is X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets.

blocks.title: Recurrence risk is a property of the genotype, not of the previous children
blocks.text: Each pregnancy of two heterozygous carriers has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child, no matter how many previous children were affected or unaffected. Genetic risk is calculated from the parents' genotypes using the rules of segregation (Punnett square) and the multiplication and addition rules for independent events.

blocks.title: Recurrence risk in an autosomal recessive condition
blocks.prompt: A couple, both carriers for phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive), have an affected first child. (a) What is the risk the next child is affected? (b) A healthy older sibling of the affected child wonders about carrier status: what is the probability that this unaffected sibling is a carrier? (c) What is the probability that of their next two children neither is affected?

blocks.markdown: **Practical points.** (1) Always consider alternatives: a single isolated case may be a **new (de novo) mutation**, or the condition may be multifactorial. (2) Pedigrees of small families may be uninformative; genetic testing can confirm the mode and identify carriers. (3) For X-linked recessive conditions, an apparently unaffected woman with an affected son and an affected brother is an **obligate carrier**. (4) Genetic counselling means explaining risks in non-directive, understandable terms so the family can make informed choices.

items: Squares male, circles female, filled affected, dot or half shading carrier; double line means consanguinity; arrow marks the proband.
AD: vertical transmission, male-to-male possible, 50% risk; AR: horizontal, parents carriers, 25% risk.
XLR: mostly males, no male-to-male transmission, carrier mother 50% of sons affected; XLD: affected father has all daughters affected, no sons.
Recurrence risks are calculated from parental genotypes and do not change with previous children.

blocks.title: Quick discriminators
blocks.text: Male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance. Two unaffected parents with an affected child of either sex suggests autosomal recessive. An affected father who transmits to all daughters but no sons suggests X-linked dominant.

points: A pedigree uses standard symbols (squares, circles, filled or dotted symbols, double line for consanguinity, arrow for the proband) to record family history across generations.
Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked patterns can be distinguished from a pedigree by generation pattern, sex ratio and the presence or absence of male-to-male transmission.
For an autosomal recessive condition two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 risk with each pregnancy; an unaffected sibling of an affected child has a 2 in 3 chance of being a carrier.

questions.stem: On a pedigree, what does a double horizontal line between a man and a woman indicate?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a double line marks a mating between blood relatives.
distractorRationale.b: Separation is shown by one or two diagonal slashes across the mating line.
distractorRationale.c: Identical twins are shown by a horizontal bar joining the two sibling lines.
distractorRationale.d: Affected status is shown by shading of the symbols.

questions.explanation: A double horizontal line between partners is the convention for consanguinity. This matters because related parents are more likely to carry the same rare recessive allele.

questions.stem: A pedigree shows affected males and females in three successive generations. An affected father has both an affected son and an affected daughter, and about half of the children of affected parents are affected. Which mode of inheritance is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vertical transmission, both sexes and male-to-male transmission at about 50% fit AD.
distractorRationale.b: Autosomal recessive conditions typically skip generations and have unaffected parents.
distractorRationale.c: X-linked recessive disease cannot pass from father to son.
distractorRationale.d: Mitochondrial inheritance is not transmitted through fathers.

questions.explanation: An affected father transmitting to a son excludes X-linked inheritance and mitochondrial inheritance. Affected individuals in every generation with about half the offspring affected is characteristic of autosomal dominant inheritance.

questions.stem: A pedigree shows three affected boys in two sibships. They are related through their mothers, who are all unaffected. There is no instance of an affected father with an affected son. Which mode of inheritance is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: affected males linked through unaffected carrier females.
distractorRationale.b: Autosomal dominant disease would affect females and show vertical transmission.
distractorRationale.c: Y-linked traits pass only from father to son.
distractorRationale.d: X-linked dominant disease would affect carrier mothers.

questions.explanation: Affected males related through unaffected females with no male-to-male transmission is the typical pattern of X-linked recessive inheritance. Carrier mothers pass the allele to half of their sons.

questions.stem: Two healthy first cousins have a child with Wilson disease. Their other relatives are unaffected. Which mode of inheritance does this family history best fit?

options.text: Autosomal recessive, with both parents being carriers

questions.correctOptionText: Autosomal recessive, with both parents being carriers

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unaffected consanguineous parents with an affected child suggest AR inheritance.
distractorRationale.b: Unaffected parents argue against a fully penetrant dominant condition.
distractorRationale.c: An affected child with unaffected parents could be XLR in a boy but Wilson disease is autosomal and affects both sexes.
distractorRationale.d: Mitochondrial inheritance would be maternal and the mother is unaffected.

questions.explanation: Consanguineous, unaffected parents with an affected child are typical of an autosomal recessive condition, as relatives are more likely to carry the same rare allele inherited from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: A man with haemophilia A (X-linked recessive) has children with a woman who is not a carrier. What is the expected outcome for their children?

options.text: All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected
All sons are affected and daughters are normal
Half of sons are affected and half of daughters are carriers

questions.correctOptionText: All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected

distractorRationale.a: Correct: he gives his X to all daughters and his Y to all sons.
distractorRationale.b: Sons receive the father's Y, not his X.
distractorRationale.c: This pattern applies to a carrier mother and an unaffected father.
distractorRationale.d: The mother is not a carrier, so no child can be affected (a daughter would need two mutant X chromosomes).

questions.explanation: A father always gives his X chromosome to his daughters, so all are obligate carriers, and his Y chromosome to his sons, who therefore inherit no mutant allele from him. The non-carrier mother contributes normal X chromosomes.

questions.stem: A couple who are both carriers of an autosomal recessive condition plan to have three children. What is the probability that at least one child is affected? Give your answer as a percentage (%).
questions.explanation: Each child is unaffected with probability 3/4, so all three are unaffected with probability (3/4)^3 = 27/64 = 0.42. The probability of at least one affected child is 1 - 27/64 = 37/64 = 0.578, or about 58%.

questions.stem: A healthy woman has a brother with an autosomal recessive condition. Both her parents are unaffected. What is the probability that she is a carrier? Give your answer as a percentage (%).
questions.explanation: Both parents must be carriers (Aa x Aa). Among their unaffected children the genotypes are AA, Aa and aA in equal numbers, so 2 of the 3 possible unaffected outcomes are carriers: 2/3, or about 66.7%.

questions.stem: True or false: An affected father with an X-linked recessive condition can pass the condition directly to his son.
questions.explanation: A father passes his Y chromosome to his sons, so X-linked traits cannot be transmitted from father to son (no male-to-male transmission). His daughters receive his X and are obligate carriers.

questions.stem: A woman, Anna, has Marfan syndrome (autosomal dominant). Her husband is unaffected. They have a son who is unaffected and a daughter who is affected. Anna's mother is affected and her father is unaffected. Describe how you would draw this three-generation pedigree, naming the symbols used for each person.
markingGuide: Generation I: unaffected father as an open square and affected mother as a filled circle joined by a horizontal mating line.
Generation II: Anna as a filled circle (with an arrow if she is the proband) and her husband as an open square, joined by a mating line.
Generation III drawn below with a vertical descent line: son as open square and daughter as filled circle, in birth order from left to right.
Roman numerals for generations and Arabic numerals for individuals.
Correct shading (filled for affected); no carrier symbols needed because the condition is dominant.
questions.explanation: A correctly drawn pedigree uses standard symbols, places generations on separate rows and joins parents to children with the descent line; the arrow identifies the proband.

questions.stem: Contrast how an autosomal recessive condition and an X-linked recessive condition appear on a pedigree, and calculate the risk to the next child in each case: (i) two carrier parents for an autosomal recessive disease; (ii) a carrier mother and an unaffected father for an X-linked recessive disease.
markingGuide: AR: unaffected carrier parents, males and females equally affected, often siblings in one generation, may involve consanguinity.
XLR: mostly males affected, transmitted through carrier females, no male-to-male transmission, skipping generations.
AR risk: Punnett square Aa x Aa gives 1/4 affected, 1/2 carrier, 1/4 unaffected non-carrier for each child regardless of previous children.
XLR carrier mother x unaffected father: 1/2 of sons affected (overall 1/4 of all children), 1/2 of daughters carriers, no daughters affected.
Statement that for each pregnancy the risk is independent.
questions.explanation: Both patterns follow from segregation of alleles: in AR each carrier parent transmits the mutant allele with probability 1/2, and in XLR the carrier mother transmits the mutant X to half of her children.
